concerns: worried because his weight has dropped by 5kg despite eating normal amounts of food

pmh: two hospitalizations for acute alcoholic pancreatitis 4 and 6 years ago, depression

clinical_knowledge.topic: Chronic Pancreatitis with Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Chronic Pancreatitis with Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes initiating pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT - e.g., Creon), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: deep upper stomach pain radiating to the back and oily stools for 6 months

Key HPI features: 6-month history of dull, continuous epigastric pain that bores through to the mid-back, partially relieved by leaning forward or sitting curled up. Reports passing bulky, pale, oily stools that float and are difficult to flush down the toilet. Recently noticed increased thirst and frequent urination.

Objective/Exam findings: Check HbA1c/fasting glucose (screen for pancreatogenic Type 3c diabetes). Abdominal exam: mild epigastric tenderness. Stool test: faecal elastase-1 (<200 ug/g confirms exocrine pancreatic insufficiency). CT abdomen or MRCP showing pancreatic calcifications, ductal dilation, and atrophy.
Relevant background/PMH: two hospitalizations for acute alcoholic pancreatitis 4 and 6 years ago, depression
Current medications: citalopram 20mg OD, paracetamol 1g QDS with limited benefit
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Chronic Pancreatitis with Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Pancreatic adenocarcinoma without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: New-onset weight loss with pancreatic pain — must exclude pancreatic cancer arising in chronic pancreatitis.
management_principles: Initiate pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT - e.g., Creon) taken with meals and snacks
Check fasting glucose and HbA1c; commence insulin/diabetic management if elevated
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 50M with 6-month history of dull, continuous epigastric pain that bores through to the mid-back, partially relieved by leaning forward or sitting curled up. Reports passing bulky, pale, oily stools that float and are difficult to flush down the toilet. Recently noticed increased thirst and frequent urination.
reference_soap.objective: Check HbA1c/fasting glucose (screen for pancreatogenic Type 3c diabetes). Abdominal exam: mild epigastric tenderness. Stool test: faecal elastase-1 (<200 ug/g confirms exocrine pancreatic insufficiency). CT abdomen or MRCP showing pancreatic calcifications, ductal dilation, and atrophy.
reference_soap.assessment: Chronic pancreatitis with exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI) and secondary endocrine diabetes (Type 3c). DDx: pancreatic adenocarcinoma, peptic ulcer disease with posterior penetration, coeliac disease.
reference_soap.plan: Initiate pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT - e.g., Creon) taken with meals and snacks. Check fasting glucose and HbA1c; commence insulin/diabetic management if elevated. Absolute abstinence from alcohol and smoking cessation support. Non-opioid pain management protocol.

learning_objectives: Identify the clinical triad of chronic pancreatitis: abdominal pain, steatorrhoea (exocrine insufficiency), and diabetes (endocrine insufficiency)
Explain the proper administration timing of pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy with meals
Assess ongoing toxic exposures (alcohol and tobacco) that accelerate pancreatic fibrosis and malignancy risk
Distinguish exocrine malabsorption symptoms from inflammatory bowel diarrhoea

teaching.diagnosis: Chronic Pancreatitis with Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency
teaching.one_liner: Repeated pancreatic inflammation, usually from alcohol, leaves scarring that can no longer make enough digestive enzymes, so fat passes through undigested as greasy, floating stools.
differentials: Peptic ulcer disease with posterior penetration
red_flags: New-onset weight loss with pancreatic pain — must exclude pancreatic cancer arising in chronic pancreatitis

must_ask.objective: Pain radiation through to the back
must_ask.say: Does the pain go through to your spine, boring straight through?
Does leaning forward or curling up ease the pain?
Are your stools oily, pale, and hard to flush away?
How much alcohol have you been drinking over the years?
Have you noticed being more thirsty or needing to urinate more often?
Are you eating your usual amount of food but still losing weight?
Have you been hospitalised for pancreatitis before?

history.answer: I've had a deep, dull ache in my upper stomach that goes right through to my back for the past six months, and my bowel motions have become pale and greasy.
The ache started gradually about six months ago, and it has been continuous almost every day since then.
It sits right in the upper middle part of my stomach, right below my ribs, and it hasn't shifted anywhere else.
Yes, it bores straight through to my mid-back like a spike going right through me.
It's a constant, deep, dull gnawing ache rather than sharp cramps or spasms.
I'd rate it around a 5 or 6 out of 10 on most days; it's a grinding pain that rarely leaves me alone.
It gets noticeably worse after eating heavy or fatty meals, but sitting curled up or leaning forward takes some of the pressure off.
I had two severe bouts of agonizing stomach pain four and six years ago that put me in the hospital with acute pancreatitis.
I feel mildly nauseated after meals at times, but I haven't actually thrown up any food, bile, or blood.
My bowel movements are bulky, pale, and oily; they float in the toilet bowl and are very difficult to flush away.
I don't have watery diarrhea or any red blood or black tarry stools, just those greasy, floating motions.
No, I haven't had any fevers, night sweats, or shivering chills.
My eyes and skin haven't turned yellow, and my urine looks normal rather than dark or tea-colored.
I don't have any burning when I pee, but I have noticed I'm constantly thirsty and have to urinate much more often, even waking up at night to go.
No, I haven't had any lightheadedness, dizzy spells, or fainting.
No chest tightness, palpitations, or shortness of breath at all.
Whenever I eat fatty or greasy food, the upper stomach pain gets worse and the oily stools become more frequent.
I take paracetamol 1 gram four times a day, but it barely helps; I haven't been taking ibuprofen, aspirin, or other painkillers.
No, I've never been told I have atrial fibrillation, irregular heartbeats, or clogged blood vessels.
My appetite has been fairly normal, but I've lost about five kilograms over the past few months without trying.
I wondered if my old stomach attacks left severe ulcer scarring in my stomach lining that won't heal.
I'm really worried about losing five kilograms even though I eat normal meals; I'm afraid my body isn't absorbing any food.
I'm hoping to get enzyme tablets to help me digest food properly and stop these oily bowel motions.
Aside from depression, I don't have high blood pressure, kidney problems, or gallstones.
I've never had surgery, but I was admitted to the hospital twice, four and six years ago, for severe alcohol-related pancreatitis.
I take citalopram 20 milligrams once daily for my mood and paracetamol 1 gram four times a day for pain; nothing else.
I don't have any known allergies to medications, foods, or materials.
I smoke about 15 cigarettes a day and have smoked for over twenty years.
I used to drink heavily, about 60 grams of alcohol daily for 20 years, though I've cut down to 10 to 15 units a week recently.
I work in warehouse logistics and live at home with my wife.
My father had high blood pressure and passed away from a stroke, but no one in my family has had pancreatic cancer, celiac disease, or bowel disorders.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 125/80 mmHg, heart rate 76 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.7°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
The patient is a middle-aged male who appears chronically fatigued and mildly uncomfortable, sitting slightly bent forward, with no acute respiratory distress.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor; sclerae are anicteric with no visible jaundice.
Abdomen is flat and symmetrical with no distension, caput medusae, visible pulsations, or surgical scars.
Normoactive bowel sounds heard throughout all four quadrants; no vascular bruits.
Soft with mild, deep tenderness elicited upon palpation in the epigastric area, with no rigidity or palpable masses.
No rebound tenderness or involuntary abdominal muscle guarding.
Negative Murphy sign with no focal right upper quadrant tenderness or inspiratory arrest.
No tenderness at McBurney point; psoas and obturator signs are negative.
Normal sphincter tone, no palpable mucosal mass or tenderness, and greasy pale stool on the glove with no frank blood.
